# 01. Discovery Interviews (AI Strategy Interviews)

Source: 8/24/2026 Rush Enterprises interviews with Kevin Provencher (GM), Jesse Welborn + Ryan Maguire (GMs), Justin Goree + Hal Meriwether (Peterbilt RGMs), Garrett Dobbs + Boston Cummings + Adam Honhera (International RGMs); and 8/25/2026 interviews with the Parts team (Joe Duncan, Kyle Bell, Jeremy Weifenbach, Shivniel Maharaj), the Aftermarket team (Chad Wellborne, Victor Cummings, Deborah Smith, Mike Eppes), IT (Asif Ansari, Daniel Decker, Matthias Schleweis), and Reporting (Jeff Johle, Marcus Demel, Robin Alizadeh, Joshua Warren, Isaac Alfaro); and the 8/27/2026 interview with the Sales leadership team (Will Waterbury, Steven Zwinggi, Adam Lesho, with sponsor Marcelo Maceira observing).

Citation tags: **[kevin]**, **[gm-1]** (Jesse and Ryan), **[peterbilt]** (Justin and Hal), **[intl]** (Garrett, Boston, Adam), **[go]**, **[check-in]** for the 8/24 files; **[parts]**, **[aftermarket]**, **[it]**, **[reporting]**, **[debrief]** for the 8/25 files; **[sales]** = `transcripts/2026-08-27-rush/interview-sales-will-steven-adam-marcelo.md`. **[inferred]** marks anything reasoned rather than observed.

**Running order, 8/24**, established by cross-references rather than by file order: International RGMs, then Kevin, then the Peterbilt RGMs, then Jesse and Ryan, then the sponsor check-in. Evidence: Grant opens the Peterbilt call with "sorry we ran a little bit late with Kevin" and "we've already spoken with a group of regional general managers" **[peterbilt]**; on the check-in he calls the Peterbilt call "second to last call today" **[check-in]**; and Lacy's remark that the interviewee who missed his slot is "in the hospital" matches Derek's absence from the Jesse and Ryan call, which she describes as "the one we just got off of" **[check-in] [gm-1]**. **Running order, 8/25**: Parts (morning), Aftermarket, IT, the internal debrief, then Reporting — with the debrief-then-Reporting step inferred; evidence is in `transcripts/2026-08-25-rush/README.md`. Order matters because several patterns depend on which call Grant was carrying context into.

This is the core skill of the workflow consultant role. The interview looks like a conversation. It is actually a structured extraction with a repeatable arc, a fixed question bank, and a set of facilitation moves. Study the arc first, then the moves.

## Two formats, one arc

The 8/24 and 8/25 batches show the same interview run in two configurations:

- **The deep-dive** (8/24): one to three field leaders, one workflow chased to the bottom, live whiteboarding, screen shares of their actual systems. The arc below was written from these.
- **The functional-group panel** (8/25): four or five corporate or functional people per call. Same monologue, same two stances, but the shape adapts. Observed panel adaptations:
  - **Get cameras on with a joke.** "I'd call it the sandwich problem. If you don't have your camera on, you could be eating a sandwich, and then I don't know if you're paying attention." **[parts]** In a five-person room, reading faces is the only way to know who is holding back a thread. On 8/27 the same sandwich bit runs as a request with a graceful opt-out instead of a roast: "if you are able to turn on your cameras, I would appreciate it. If not, I understand. Sometimes you're just eating a sandwich and you don't want to put your camera on. I get it." **[sales]** The ask stays; the pressure is optional.
  - **Map the roles before the pain.** "where are your guys' roles similar and overlapping and different? Can you just give me a high-level overview of that so I know how to target my questions?" **[parts]** A panel wastes its hour if you ask the corporate roll-up owner the branch questions and vice versa.
  - **Go around the horn, in visible order, and say the order.** "in the order that I see you on my screen, it's going to go Joe, Kyle, and Jeremy" **[parts]**; "I'm going to randomly select order here. I'm going to go Chad, Victor, Deborah, Mike. That's the order on my screen. So have fun with it." **[aftermarket]** Announcing the queue lets everyone else relax and listen instead of rehearsing.
  - **Park and return, explicitly.** Each first answer gets acknowledged and banked, not chased: "I'm going to come back with other questions, but that's a good jumping-off point" **[parts]**; "Chad, you're off the hook for right now. I'll circle back to you." **[aftermarket]** The deep dives start only after the full round.
  - **Apologize for the buzzwords up front.** "my line of business has a lot of buzzwords. So I apologize if I sound like all the AI ads you might see on a billboard... but I promise I'm well-intentioned." **[aftermarket]**, repeated as an "umbrella apology" on **[it]**. Disarms the corporate audience the way the note-taking joke disarms the field audience.

## The arc of the call

1. **Rapport open (under 2 minutes).** Weather, location, a light joke. On 8/24: Louisville sunshine with Kevin **[kevin]**, and "do people make jokes that you're in Boston?" with Boston Cummings **[intl]**. Small, human, fast.
2. **A version of "do you know what we're doing on today's call?"** Asked at the top of every interview where the opening is captured, though the wording moves. Kevin got "do you know what you're doing on today's call?" **[kevin]**, Justin and Hal got "do you have a good idea of what we're doing on today's call?" **[peterbilt]**, the International group got "do you guys know what we're doing on this call here today?" **[intl]**, Jesse and Ryan got "how much information do you have on why we're on this call?" **[gm-1]**, and the Parts panel got "does everyone know what we're doing on today's call? Why we're here? Sort of?" — answered with "sort of," which he accepts and works with: "All right. I can work with sort of." **[parts]** The Sales panel got the sixth phrasing — "How much context do we have as to what we're doing on this call today?" — answered with "A little bit, I think," which he banks the same way: "I've heard worse answers, so I'll take that," before explaining why the question exists at all: "a lot of times I get blank stares on that one because it's easy to set up a call on someone's calendar and say, hey, this guy's going to talk to you and ask you a bunch questions." **[sales]** Never assume the client briefed their people. It resets the room, gives permission to say no, and tells you how much context-setting the monologue needs. He softens it too: "It's okay to say no. A lot of times I get blank faces." **[intl]** Partial context is fine; he fills the gap ("How about I fill in some dots") rather than making anyone feel unprepared. **[parts]**
3. **The opening monologue (90 seconds to two minutes, semi-scripted).** See the annotated version below. On the Kevin call it draws a compliment and a self-deprecating admission in the same beat: "That's my big opening monologue." / "You did good." / "Thanks. It's a little bit rehearsed." **[kevin]** Fathom's speaker labels are scrambled across that exchange, so treat the split as best-reading rather than certain, but the compliment reads as Kevin's and the "rehearsed" admission as Grant's **[inferred]**. Rehearsed is fine. Rehearsed is the point.
4. **Pro Complainer question.** "What are the things that drain your time and energy right now?" Offered as broadly as possible, with permission to go anywhere: "It could be anything and everything under the sun." **[kevin]**
5. **Pull the first thread.** Whatever they name first gets the deep dive. "Amazing. So let's pull on that thread." **[kevin]**
6. **Map the workflow live.** Whiteboard with boxes and arrows on the second screen, often screen-shared. He narrates a deliberately rough draft of their process and asks them to fix it. "My love language is recognizing arrows, and it's not my wife's favorite thing, but it does help me in my job." **[kevin]**
7. **Get into the real systems.** "Can you show us some of the things that you've built?" **[gm-1]** He wants to see Service Connect, the WIP board, the actual spreadsheet, the UltiPro queue. Watching someone work beats hearing them describe it.
8. **Mid-call checkpoint (around the halfway mark).** "But I'm also happy we got half an hour left. How can I make this call the most useful to you?" **[kevin]** The same move lands on the Jesse and Ryan call: "we've got about half an hour left. I do have questions about sales, but... what do you guys think would be more useful?" **[gm-1]** He offers to keep going or zoom out. This hands control back and surfaces the interviewee's own priority ranking.
9. **Cross-call loop closing.** He carries open questions between interviews and says so: "the reason I'm talking about this is because it came up in a previous call. So I'm trying to just make sure I close all my open loops here." **[gm-1]** By the fourth interview of the day he is pattern-matching across the org in real time, and says so out loud when asked for recurring themes.
10. **Close.** Recap the opportunities in their language, tell them what happens next (survey, follow-up questions, findings "in about three, four weeks" **[peterbilt]**), release them warmly ("you're off the hook" **[kevin]**), and leave the door open ("I'm an email away" **[intl]**). The 8/27 close adds three beats worth copying: the destination artifact gets named with its audience and clock ("a presentation, which will go up to Jody in about three weeks" and "what is the AI strategy in one sentence, and then what does that look like in a 12 month rollout"); the room is recruited into that artifact ("if there's anything that you want in that presentation that's going to Jody... by all means, don't hold back"); and the relationship gets a physical next touchpoint ("we're going to see each other at the bar in San Antonio"). He also banks goodwill by ending early: "I'll let you out a few minutes early here." **[sales]**

## The opening monologue, annotated

Beats observed across the 8/24 interviews. The first four beats appear on all four of those calls; the last two vary, so they are marked. The 8/25 calls carry the same beats where the opening is captured (**[parts]**, **[aftermarket]**, **[it]**; Reporting's opening is missing from the transcript), with wording notes below the table.

| Beat | Example language | Where | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| Identity | "my name's Grant. I am the CEO. A company called GPC and also the Workflow Consultant that is working with Rush to understand how does AI fit into the business." | All four | Authority plus hands-on. Not a salesperson, the actual practitioner. |
| Mission frame | "we start with the people because ultimately the people are not going anywhere and we want AI to be a complement, not a replacement." | All four, fullest on **[kevin]** | Disarms the unspoken fear in the room before anyone has to voice it. |
| Method | "How is it created? How is it delegated? How is it completed? And how is it marked as complete?... because if we can decompose how work works, we can reimagine it with more AI in the middle." | All four | Gives the interviewee a mental model for what a useful answer looks like. |
| The two stances | Pro Complainer ("what are the things that drain your time and energy") and Pro Dreamer ("magic wand, all your dreams come true"). | All four | Sets up the whole call as two simple questions anyone can answer. |
| Note-taking disclosure | "if you see me looking into the distance, I promise I'm not playing a video game. I'm very presently, fervently taking notes for you." | **[kevin] [peterbilt] [intl]**. On **[gm-1]** he says only "I'm a fast typer and I got a little whiteboard over here. I'm taking notes," with no joke attached. | Kills the distracted-consultant read before it forms. |
| Team intro | "we've got Olivia here, who's a new workflow consultant as well on the team, just kind of listening and sharing." | One sentence on **[kevin]**. On **[intl]** Olivia introduces herself in full. On **[peterbilt]** Grant flags that she is between calls and will join late. On **[gm-1]** she is let in from the waiting room without an introduction. On **[parts]** she is "training as a new workflow consultant, so she'll be shadowing." | Normalizes the second person in the room. |

Pre-SOW variant, 7/15 Delta data review call **[delta-data 1:50]**: the same monologue runs on a sales call, compressed. Identity ("I'm the CEO of GPC. I'm Pete's business partner"), the four questions ("how does work get created, delegated, completed, and marked as complete. So I see digital assembly lines everywhere"), the two stances by name ("the pro-dreamer, pro-complainer mentality"), and the trust rationale said to the prospect's face: "if I can make people's lives easier, they're much more likely to trust us and tell us more and allow us into their walled garden... this engagement, if we do get to work together, is all about establishing trust with the people on your team so that we can change the way they work." It opens with a consent check and an agenda ask ("Does that sound like an okay plan? And does anyone have any other objectives that they wanted to share today") and a name-pronunciation check. Same beats, same order, a year of engagements earlier in the relationship.

8/25 wording notes: the mission frame gains a third verb set — "we want to use AI to multiply human creativity, strategy, and relationships, not subtract by any means, but also not replace just a two-person swap" **[parts]**, and "we're trying to multiply your strategy, your creativity, your problem solving" **[aftermarket]**. The note-taking disclosure survives in panel form ("if you see me staring off in the distance over here, I've got a little whiteboard digital thing that I'm working on" **[parts]**). And the shadow is no longer silent: on 8/25 Olivia asks her own extraction questions (her SOP question on the Parts call produced the tribal-knowledge ratio, one of the day's biggest findings), takes delegated follow-ups live ("Olivia, want to follow up with Chad, just in an email" **[aftermarket]**), and gets deferred to as the authority on SEC data handling ("Olivia does much better than I do, so I'm not going to touch that" **[reporting]**). The second-chair role is a real interviewing role, not a listening role.

8/27 wording notes: the monologue now folds in the process-therapist frame and pre-absolves the complaining ("I say complaining willingly, because people think of us as their kind of process therapists") and closes with an explicit consent check — "Questions on that? All right. Rock and roll." **[sales]** The team intro upgrades Olivia from shadow to peer: "Olivia is another consultant on our team." **[sales]** The second chair also gets the note-capture delegation live in front of the client: "Olivia, if you can make a note on that, I think that'd be a fantastic demo that we can prepare." **[sales]** (She has no labeled turns in this transcript; see the folder README.)

## The question bank

Questions observed on 8/24, grouped by what they extract. Quoted text is the transcript wording.

**Openers:**
- "What are the things that drain your time and energy right now?" **[all interviews]**
- "what does it look like in your role if you wave a magic wand and all your dreams come true?" **[kevin]**
- The repeating-task version: "What are the tasks, the processes, the things that you're like, Oh, I got to do this again? Ideally repeating." **[parts]**
- Panel targeting, before any pain question: "where are your guys' roles similar and overlapping and different?... so I know how to target my questions" **[parts]**
- When someone offers two menus of pain: "Where's the pain the sharpest? And then we'll go from highest to... more mild." **[aftermarket]**

**Workflow tracing:**
- "So where do I have it wrong?" **[kevin]**
- "if I were to do high level, it'd be like, I've got a problem, I generate a quote, I take your car, I fix your car, I order parts, I get my parts, I fix your car, I give it back, right? There's probably more detail to that." **[kevin]**
- "what does that sales process look like?" **[kevin]**, then replays the answer back as stages
- "what's the information that you need during those handoffs" **[kevin]**
- "what do those teams continually go back and forth and go, Kevin, I'm missing this. I really need, like, I can't move this forward until I have that. What comes to mind?" **[kevin]**
- "what does that look like when you make one of those? Like, are you exporting a file and then cleaning it up?" **[peterbilt]**
- "Can you explain to me what happens upstream of the need to process a part or an order? And then what happens downstream?" **[parts]**
- "what does it mean to actually make a report tactically? Because in my mind, it means I'm exporting data with specific sets of filters, and then I'm manually manipulating that data" — a draft-it-wrong offered in words instead of boxes **[reporting]**
- "when you say conflicting data... can you take me through any example, most recent one that comes to mind?" followed by "I want to know explicit, like, names" of the tools **[reporting]**
- The tooling day-in-the-life: "what tools are you using in the sales process? Do we have zoom info?... are we recording calls or calls happening on... company phones, private phones, walk me through day in the life of an average rep from a technology perspective" — announced as "a little bit boring" and asked anyway **[sales]**
- The segmentation probe, with candidate answers offered: "how do we cut up our market map?... How do we cut up the market? Industry-based, fleet size solely? Does one person just use school buses? Talk to me about that." **[sales]**

**Systems and data:**
- "Where is your WIP management stored? What is the source of truth?" **[intl]**
- "who owns the marketing or slash... sales communication tools?... Lacy, do you know who the owner of that is?" **[kevin]**, which turns a tool into a named person
- "what's feeding that? Is that Service Connect?" and "is this something that's inside of Service Connect? SAP? Is it a sprint? Is it an Excel file?" **[peterbilt]**
- "Can you show me all the statuses that a WIP could be in?" **[intl]**
- "those calls are recorded right now or no?" **[gm-1]**
- "Can other people access this and update it?" **[gm-1]**
- "when you talk about going and grabbing those OE processes, is that password-gated or is that public information?" **[aftermarket]**
- "And all that data lives in which platform? Is that SAP?" **[aftermarket]**
- "Where's the software development lifecycle stored? Is that Jira?" **[it]**
- For anything the client built themselves: "What is the adoption process? What is the procurement process if you were to say, yes, this is working?... How does that become canon?" **[it]**
- The fields-that-matter question, asked of managers rather than admins: "What CRM fields are genuinely useful for you in your roles for you to see from the reps...? Because I know there's a lot of fluff in a CRM. And so I want to try to understand what are the things that move the needle for you or for the sales process? And I see those as two different things." **[sales]** It produced Will's full ideal-customer-profile spec (fleet size by class, OE mix, powertrain, fleet age, SAP account number, purchase history, health status, integrated parts/service spend) plus an offered follow-up artifact ("I can send this to you guys in an email or a word doc").
- The catalog question, for tribal trigger knowledge: "do you have a catalog of some of these potential cycles of, Hey, we should have a conversation, meaning financing triggers, warranties going out, your average truck lifetime?... This is tribal knowledge that I would love to become corporate company knowledge," pressed with "So what are some of those other triggers?" **[sales]**

**Sizing and signals:**
- "we're trying to collect what is the size of the prize? What are the things that they take a lot of time to do every instance, the things that happen very frequently, and then that creates a larger kind of value equation." **[gm-1]**
- The clean in-room version arrived on 8/25 (superseding an earlier note here that no tight phrasing had been observed): "I would love to try to narrow it down to the one that you feel like has the largest value multiple, which means the time it takes you to do it, the frequency at which you do it. So one monthly report that takes you eight hours, it would have an answer of eight, versus something that takes you three hours every week would be 12. So what comes to your mind when you think about that total, that big beast?" **[reporting]**
- The economics probe, flagged as indulgence so it never reads as a challenge: "let's just quickly humor me. Can you explain the numbers behind no-move inventory in terms of what that costs?... Just humor me." **[parts]** It surfaced the reserve mechanics (0.5 percent at nine months, write-off at 24) and the $20 million sizing.
- "Quick poll the room, where are WIP logs looking like for Adam and Garrett?" **[intl]**
- "what are the signals for proactive action?" **[intl]**
- For builders: "Where do you see your technical limit or your time and bandwidth being limited right now?" **[gm-1]**
- The density check that scales a later opportunity: "How many accounts does the average rep manage?" **[sales]** (Answer: managed accounts start at 20 trucks; an average level-two rep carries "probably 25 to maybe 100" accounts after a cleansing purge of billboard accounts.)
- The mechanism test, inviting the client to kill the idea: "if I were to make an account manager better at... having knowledge about their accounts, do you think that would help the total number of sales? Like, does being more informed help increase our cross-sell, up-sell, or do you think it's just the nature of the business and that won't really help?" **[sales]** Ask whether the lever actually moves the outcome before sizing the lever.
- "How much does seasonality play into your business?" — a demand-shape probe; the room upgraded the word for him ("I wouldn't call it as much seasonality as cyclical"). **[sales]** (The question is filed under Steven's label by Fathom; context makes it Grant's — see the folder README.)

**Friction and politics:**
- "can we get just a little bit more naming names? So like, you don't have to be people specific, but like, this department doesn't want me in this tool would be amazing." **[it]** Asked after a generic complaint about access; it produced the specific team, the PR-gate story, and the workaround tech debt.
- "when you were looking at their GitHub, were they not okay with you having read-only access?" — pinning down exactly where a permission fight actually sits **[it]**

**Temperature and close:**
- "do you think the team is fearful of AI? Excited about AI? Confused? What's the general temperature of the room?" **[intl]**
- "What is the mood in the room, this room and larger, about chat-based LLM tools?... What is the general sentiment?" **[aftermarket]**
- "there anything that you guys didn't get to say today that you wanted to?" **[intl]**
- The primed version of the same close, once the room has learned what a useful answer looks like: "now that you know what we're looking for... is there anything that the group would like to share or ask now that you know what type of information we're looking for?" **[reporting]**, echoed on **[parts]** ("now that you know what we're looking for, you're dreaming and you're like, oh my gosh, Grant, got to tell them, shoot it to us in an email") and **[it]** ("things that they want to get off their chest before I wrap up").

## Facilitation moves (the craft)

**Draft it wrong on purpose.** He sketches their workflow fast and imperfectly, then asks "where do I have it wrong?" People correct a wrong diagram far more readily and precisely than they answer a blank question. The Kevin call is a masterclass: the entire sales-to-fulfillment flow came out of iterative correction of Grant's rough boxes. **[kevin]**

**Let them ramble, then absolve them.** Kevin apologized twice for rambling. Grant: "No, if you're rambling too much or off-stream, I'll cut you off. But for us, this is discovery, right? This is us going down a rabbit hole and seeing what's in there and then coming back and popping up to the next opportunity." **[kevin]** Hal got the same absolution on the Peterbilt call after "I'm sorry if I'm talking too much": "You're doing just fine. Don't worry." **[peterbilt]** Rambling is where the real pain lives. Protect it.

**Name the emotion, lightly.** The therapy frame on the International call came from the interviewees first. After the three RGMs unloaded, Grant asked "That feel good?" and Adam replied "We should have warned you that we probably all need therapy," which Grant took and ran with: "People often call me a process therapist." **[intl]** He reuses the frame later on the same call ("one of the questions I had from when you guys were in your therapy session") and closes with "Hopefully it felt good to get some of that stuff off your chest." **[intl]** Humor keeps a complaint session from curdling into a gripe session. Note that the move here is picking up the client's own joke, not supplying one.

**Replay their words back as structure.** After a long winding answer from Kevin, Grant returns: "I see it as as discovery, spec-ing, so the process of designing a truck, quote and negotiate. So when we start talking about money, out for signature, closed won, closed lost." **[kevin]** He converts mess into stages, then asks for a verdict: "How does this feel?" **[kevin]** Boston's WIP walkthrough got the same treatment: "huge opportunity in what I'm going to call the status mismatch workflow." **[intl]**

**Chase the mental model until it clicks.** The VIN exchange with Jesse is the pattern: Grant thought the VIN pulled Service Connect data, the answer didn't add up, and he kept asking ("So why did you paste it here if the system is not connected to Service Connect?") until his model matched reality, then narrated the correction back. **[gm-1]** Never nod through confusion. A wrong mental model poisons every recommendation downstream.

**Give a framework, then hand it to them.** Small teaching moments planted mid-call: required CRM fields must serve forecasting or reporting or they should be optional **[kevin]**; deal stages are changes of responsibility **[kevin] [gm-1]**; BANT for quote-stage qualification, which he names as "budget, authority, need, and timeline... that's just a classic, call that the BANT framework" **[kevin]**; double opt-in handoffs between sales and service and parts **[kevin]**; tier-one support augmentation, where the shoe-order example lands as "You don't need the CEO answering that. You want the fastest response with my tracking code" **[intl]**. These position GPC as advisors, not just note-takers, and they give the client vocabulary they'll repeat back later.

**Be honest about limits, in the moment.** "I can't impact those dependencies in the software that they've built... in the sales process, that would be, that's outside of our current controls." **[kevin]** And on Outlook: "Chances are we're not going to get drafting emails in Outlook just from a data security perspective, want to set my expectations properly." **[peterbilt]** Refusing to overpromise in the room is what makes the promises you do make credible.

**Name artifacts precisely.** He captures exact file names on the call: "2026-0824-New-DSA and Corp.AR-07-13-26-Read-Only" **[peterbilt]**, which he repeats back on the check-in hours later to anchor the demo request **[check-in]**. Vague notes ("they have some reports") die after the call. Named artifacts become follow-up emails, then demo material.

**Check the room before switching threads.** "I do have questions about sales, but when you think about opportunities right now... what do you guys think would be more useful?" **[gm-1]** and "Do we want to stick with what we've been talking about... Both answers are fine. Just need to know," which Kevin answers with "Let's see where you take it first." **[kevin]** He offers the fork, they choose, engagement stays high.

**Triage the unique case out of the room.** New on 8/25, and worth studying. Robin's SEC reporting workflow was clearly real and clearly unlike everyone else's, so ten minutes in Grant cut him loose: "I'm going to do you solid. I'm going to say you probably don't need to be here... to make any other meaningful Q&A, I would need to exclude the rest of the group," paired with a flattery cushion ("you are very special here"), a booked follow-up ("let's have an email conversation to get some time on the calendar for next week"), and the standard release ("You're off the hook"). **[reporting]** The panel keeps its pace, the specialist feels prioritized rather than dismissed, and the follow-up call will get a full hour instead of a squeezed fragment. The tell that triggers it: "your use case will be very unique."

**Test yesterday's hypothesis on today's room.** He converts findings from earlier calls into predictions and checks them out loud: "if there's anything I got from yesterday's calls, it's that you guys get a lot of emails. Is that true?" — answered with "500 a day." **[parts]** And he replays structures for verification, not just color: the deal stages captured from the GMs get read back to the CRM manager, who corrects their scope ("I think that might be more aftermarket... in truck sales, it's a little more granular"). **[reporting]** Day two of an engagement is for validating day one, and saying so ("we're trying to connect dots between what's going on in this call, the calls we had yesterday, the other calls that we'll have" **[parts]**).

**Harvest the variables live.** When an opportunity crystallizes, he builds the spec in the room by listing the decision variables back and asking for the missing ones: "So I took down a few variables... I see that it's in stock, there's five units, they want three... how fast would it be to get here, what are the freight fees, am I taking those or are you taking those... is it on a no sale list... what are some of these other variables that would go into that recommendation?" **[parts]** The room added two (national availability across branches, down payments on special orders). The interviewees co-author the requirements without ever being asked "what are your requirements."

**Sketch the solution shape, then take it back.** On 8/25 he allows himself one light concrete image once a pain is fully drawn — "I kind of imagine there being like a little widget on here, like a little info icon that says insight or action" **[parts]** — but immediately re-anchors ownership: "it's not about you guys knowing what's technically possible. It's about us knowing what would make your lives easier, and then we'll take care of the technicals." **[parts]** The sketch tests resonance; it is never a commitment. This refines rather than contradicts the no-pitching rule below. The 8/27 version sketches from the room's own raw material — "if we could take a picture of a company's car and grab their fleet size... we can have a workflow, find the Department of Transportation number and grab the fleet size and potentially route that into the CRM" — and takes it back the same way: "we'll use technology to match the need. You guys don't need to worry about that kind of thing. Does that make sense?" **[sales]**

**Know what not to pitch, and close the door out loud.** The AI pricing companion idea got tested against reality — "is there publicly available information that you could be doing competitor analysis, or is that not really a thing?" — and when Joe answered "Not really a thing," Grant dropped it in the room rather than carrying a dead idea into the readout. **[parts]** Same move as the 8/24 Outlook expectation-setting: refusing an opportunity is itself a credibility deposit.

**Offer the safe path to the sensitive artifact.** When Jeff hesitated to screen-share ("obviously it's sensitive data... I can't show you"), Grant didn't push and didn't drop it: he named the NDA already in place, disclaimed what he didn't know ("If you've got stuff that's going to the SEC, I don't know their rules. Olivia does much better than I do, so I'm not going to touch that"), and let Jeff invent the compliant version himself — "I could show you maybe a prior month just as a sample." **[reporting]** The artifact still gets seen; nobody's compliance instincts get overridden.

**Protect the off-record remark.** When Matthias vented about another team and said "hopefully I'm not getting quoted," Grant made the handling explicit: "I will not quote you, but I may use your quote and own it myself," and later, "I will make sure that that gets communicated in the right way with some taste, with some tactical positioning." **[it]** Interviews only stay honest if people can safely say the impolitic thing. Absorb it, launder the attribution, deliver the substance.

**Meet a fluent room with the open kimono.** The Aftermarket group was IT-fluent, so mid-call Grant zoomed out and turned the interview partly into co-strategy: he taught the skill-file concept in plain terms ("A skill is a text file with a name, a description, and a body. Anyone can write one."), explained the engagement's real mechanics (the three-six-twelve-month priority list, high-impact/low-effort sorting), and then recruited them against their own blockers: "How can I help you undo your blockers you're giving to me by presenting you with a strategy we can all align to?... End of monologue. How are we feeling?" **[aftermarket]** With a room that can obstruct or accelerate the eventual recommendation, discovery includes discovering what will get it approved. Note the self-aware label — he calls his own teaching stretch a monologue and asks for a temperature check right after.

**Let the observer break their own rule, then harvest it.** New on 8/27. Marcelo (the sponsor) attends the Sales panel as a self-declared observer, and twenty minutes in asks permission to break the seal: "I know I'm supposed to observe, but I would like to add something here." Grant lets him — the intervention delivers the customer-profile vision and the market-data diagnosis, arguably the call's densest two minutes — and then wires it into the room rather than letting it float: "Okay, real quick string I want to pull on," then later "The first part of what Marcelo was saying earlier..." (picked up by Will), and "to connect the dot back to what Marcelo was talking about." By @37:09 the observer is a directly addressable source: "maybe Marcelo, you can answer this one." **[sales]** A sponsor in the room is not furniture; treat their interjection as testimony and their presence as an escalation path for feasibility questions (the LA export got a same-second "Yeah" because the person who could authorize it was already there).

**Book the demo in the room.** When a pain has a concrete dataset and its owner is present, convert it to a demo request before the call ends: "If I asked for an export of your current account list for one of the demos that we prepare in LA, would that be feasible? Yeah. Awesome. I'll follow up on that. Olivia, if you can make a note on that." **[sales]** On 8/24 demo candidates were chosen hours later on the sponsor check-in **[check-in]**; by 8/27 the conversion happens live, with the note-capture delegated in the same breath. The demo is also aimed at the client's own stated goal (the LA untapped-market thread), not at a generic showpiece.

**Show them the board.** The note-taking disclosure has an endgame: mid-call he screen-shares the working whiteboard and explains its color code — "the red ones are the questions that are the pain points, purple is our questions for you, and then yellow is the opportunities that we see" — as the level-set before the opportunities recap. **[sales]** The board that made him look distracted at minute two makes the method visible at minute forty; the room sees their complaints already sorted into a work product.

## Adapting to interviewee types

Four archetypes showed up on 8/24 and six more on 8/25. The archetype labels are the playbook's framing **[inferred]**; the behavior under each is observed. The arc stays the same, the emphasis shifts.

| Archetype | 8/24 example | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| The process complainer | Kevin (GM, Tampa) **[kevin]** | Give him the whiteboard. Draft his process wrong, let him fix it, hand him the diagram as a gift ("I can give you these diagrams and maybe you use those in the Tampa situation"). His pain is your map. |
| The citizen builder | Jesse (GM, Cleveland) **[gm-1]**, identified as "my GM in Cleveland" by Adam on the earlier International call **[intl]**; Will Waterbury (Sales) **[sales]** | Ask for a demo immediately. Get the numbers in his words: kickbacks down 30 percent and claimable amount up 17 percent, over two months of use. Ask where his technical limit and bandwidth end, because that's where GPC starts. Inspect the knowledge base structure. He is a future champion and a governance case study. Will is the corporate-manager variant: two working Claude prompts (CRM-scorecard coaching, competitor-pricing sourcing), self-deprecating about it ("don't laugh at me when I say this"), asking for token-efficiency training and a controlled distribution path rather than a free sandbox — his asks are the governance proposal's requirements, verbatim. **[sales]** |
| The new-in-role leader | Ryan (GM, month two) **[gm-1]** | Mine the fresh eyes. "I'd be curious to hear how your experience in use trucks is affecting the way you see the picture right now." New leaders see friction that veterans have normalized. |
| The power operator | Hal, Justin **[peterbilt]**, Boston, Garrett, Adam **[intl]** | Follow them into the weeds. Watch them run their actual morning: the GP sheet, the WIP filter, the receivables dig, the UltiPro queue. Quantify the saturation with them, the way Boston did unprompted: 3,363 open ROs across the three regions, four ROs per minute at peak, roughly 14 hours to comb through them all. **[intl]** Their job is information routing, your job is to see every route. |
| The corporate roll-up owner | Joe Duncan (Director of Parts Operations, 37 years, 182 locations) **[parts]** | He sees every branch's dashboard at the all-branch level and hunts anomalies across "tens of thousands of lines." Ask for the screen share, then ask what a magic wand looks like *for the branch users*, not for him — he will redirect the question to his people himself ("this is your opportunity to say, you know what I would really like"). Get him to explain the economics behind the KPI; he owns the reserve math. |
| The report builder | Jeff Johle, Marcus Demel **[reporting]** | Their pain is a named beast: a monthly report with a day of assembly, 12–15 source tabs, upstream data dependencies that pin the calendar. Get the beast named, sized with the value-multiple math, and shown on screen (via the safe-sample path if the data is sensitive). Ask what's upstream — the real finding is often the dependency chain (financials post the 12th–15th, payroll mid-month), not the assembly labor. Listen for doubt about the report's purpose ("I've sat in these meetings and I personally, I don't know what the value is") — that's a finding too. |
| The unique-case specialist | Robin Alizadeh (SEC reporting) **[reporting]** | Do them a solid: release them from the group call and book a dedicated hour. Their workflow will not generalize to the room, and the room's time will not do their case justice. |
| The blocked builder | Asif Ansari **[it]** | Already shipping with AI at full speed (a thousand BW-to-Snowflake query translations, a year of human work, done in two months with Claude Code) and hitting organizational walls, not technical ones: PR gates rejecting AI-written code, access "kumbaya moments," workaround workspaces accruing tech debt. Ask for names of the friction points ("naming names"). Their blockers map the org's real governance gaps better than any policy document. |
| The in-house ally | Daniel Decker **[it]** | Doing a version of GPC's own job from the inside (FDE-style team, skills, intake funnel, CoE ambitions). Do not compete; inventory. "A lot of the things that we typically recommend sounds like you're already active on, which is great... We don't care if we're the ones that build it." Ask how their things become canon, ask to see their artifacts, and position GPC as the connective layer they don't have bandwidth for (Daniel has three people). |
| The burned veteran | Matthias Schleweis **[it]** | Has stopped asking other teams for anything ("we learned not to reach out to other teams to ask for anything anymore, if you want to do progress") and vents only when invited and protected. Their scar tissue is a map of every failed cross-team route; the off-record handling move is written for them. |

## What you're listening for (extraction checklist)

Run this list mentally during every interview. Each item traces to something said on 8/24.

- Repeated tasks with a frequency and a duration attached **[intl] [peterbilt]**
- Copy and paste, export, filter, snip, and "I carve out my region" workflows. Justin: "I do a lot of snip, copy, and paste, and then explain the actual item." **[peterbilt]**
- Report-to-decision chains: which report, which decision, which next action **[peterbilt] [intl]**
- Anomaly hunting. Hal's Long Beach store "took a $60,000 hit because somebody input a price of a bucket of oil" **[peterbilt]**, and Jacques "has this just ridiculous ability to find the one RO that somehow has slipped through all the cracks" **[intl]**
- Status mismatches between systems or between a status field and reality **[intl]**
- Information routing burdens: who forwards what to whom, and what commentary they add. Adam: "I'm literally just slicing out the Excel thing and putting it in and then forwarding it on to the people who need to understand it." **[intl]**
- Handoff failures between departments, and what information goes missing in them **[kevin]**
- The source of truth for every workflow mentioned **[intl]**
- Existing self-built tools, with their real usage numbers **[gm-1]**
- Data access constraints: permissions, licenses, firewalls. Jesse: "the biggest issue that I've run into, limitation-wise, is permissions and access granted for others." **[gm-1]** Adam: "it's either behind a firewall or it's not consistent in the way it's being produced." **[intl]** Marcelo, on the sponsor call: "we wish we could record stuff, but IT doesn't let us." **[check-in]**
- Email volume and triage rules. Adam: "if it's past the third line in the email, I probably miss the action item that you had in there." **[intl]** Confirmed as an org-wide constant on 8/25: Joe's "500 a day" **[parts]**, and Olivia's debrief summary, "Every single person on every single call said, there's too many emails, too many reports." **[debrief]**
- The tribal-knowledge ratio. Olivia's question — when a report demands an action, where do the instructions live? — got "10-90. 10% written down, 90% is tribal knowledge... In people's head, we hope." **[parts]** Ask it about any process; the answer sizes both the automation risk and the onboarding opportunity.
- Conflicting metric definitions across systems. Joshua's service-revenue example: five reports, five definitions (labor only; labor plus machine sales; everything billed; only active techs; only customer labor), "and they all just say, this was service revenue." **[reporting]** When two systems disagree, ask whether it's the data or the definition.
- Shadow AI and token starvation. Robin remote-logging into a home computer with a personal Claude license because "I'm like Tiny Tim for tokens right now" **[reporting]**; Asif having "run the bill to the highest amount that it's ever been at Rush" **[it]**. Both directions — starvation and blowout — are demand signals, and Grant names the pattern in the room: "the Shadow IT thing is something that we're hearing around the room." **[reporting]**
- Cross-team access friction. The PR gate that rejected AI-generated code, the "kumbaya moment" meetings before any access grant, the separate workspace built as a workaround. **[it]** Every workaround someone built to route around another team is a governance finding.
- Turnover and onboarding load. Deborah: "We put someone on the counter on day one, and we're like, go sell some parts. They don't know what the systems are... they're just hoping that the guy next to them gives them all of the instructions." **[aftermarket]** High-turnover roles are where an always-on onboarding coach beats another dashboard.
- Exceptions with a dollar figure attached. The $10,000 unanswered warranty claim **[reporting]**, the $1,000–$2,500 per day of truck downtime against a $1,700 average repair bill **[aftermarket]**, the 0.5 percent no-move reserve **[parts]**. An exception someone can price is an opportunity someone will fund.
- Problems AI cannot fix, so you can say so. Competitor-quote-driven pricing with no public data ("it's essentially a race to zero... Not really a thing" **[parts]**) died in the room, on purpose.
- Untracked trigger events — dates the business already knows that should start a conversation and don't: financing contracts expiring, fleet trade-in cycles ("they'll buy their 50 trucks, they'll trade them at four years and 400,000 miles, and it's very predictive"), warranty run-outs. Will: "If someone financed the truck with us and that contract's about to expire, we should be automating that." **[sales]** Ask whether a catalog of the triggers exists; on 8/27 the answer was "We do not centrally manage that today. I believe we have the data to make us capable of doing that." **[sales]**
- Where activity is instrumented versus invisible, inside the same company. Rush truck-sales reps run on personal cell phones and personal vehicles (untrackable); the aftermarket sales team runs company vehicles with Geotab pinging arrival at customer locations, feeding daily performance metrics. **[sales]** The instrumented sibling team is both the proof of feasibility and the template.
- External data the client must manually launder before trusting. Polk registration data is skewed by tax-incentive registration ("you'll see Maine on the trailer, and of course Indiana's the biggest... Indianapolis is like the largest market on the planet"), RigDigBI is "not always accurate," and reps validate fleets by DOT number on safersys.org — five years into defining their own markets, "probably like 70% to defining our markets." **[sales]** A data source everyone uses and nobody trusts is a workflow finding, not a data finding.
- Data quality as an incentive problem, not a systems problem. Reps "pencil whip" CRM activity logs; well-paid veterans "just don't have to" ("you look at your checking account, it's very strong"); Marcelo's blunt version: "we mostly or totally depend on the reps to complete information about a customer and they're lazy." **[sales]** When the field's rational incentives produce the bad data, the fix is capture automation or coaching cadence, not another required field.
- Emotional heat. The louder the sigh, the bigger the prize. **[inferred]** The 8/27 tell: Steven's "my eyes bleed sometimes when I start talking through this" (attribution scrambled by Fathom — see the folder README) and "it'd probably scare you how many deals we lost over the last 10 or 15, 20 years," which Grant absorbs without flinching: "It won't scare me. I've seen pretty bad things." **[sales]**

## What never happens in these calls

- No product pitching. Grant does describe what a workflow could do when he summarizes an opportunity, and on 8/25 he occasionally sketches a solution shape to test resonance (the insight-or-action widget **[parts]**), but he does not sell a tool, and he says why: "That's why I rarely talk about AI in these calls, because that's not the focus." **[kevin]** The 8/25 statement of the same rule: "we're happy without proposing any solutions because that's not the goal of this call." **[it]** One near-exception is on record: at the very end of the IT call, prompted by the client's own vendor-evaluation talk, he named GPC's preferred governance vendor with a joke ("ours rhymes with Avocado") **[it]** — and then second-guessed exactly that reveal in the debrief. See module 04.
- No solutioning commitments in the room. Opportunities get noted ("Noted on that one as well" **[kevin]**), not promised.
- No skipping the monologue, the complainer question, or the closing recap, even when time is short. Observed on all interviews whose openings are captured (the Reporting transcript starts mid-call, so its opening cannot be checked).
- No pretending to understand. Confusion gets chased until it resolves. **[gm-1]**
- No letting a call end without knowing what happens next and who owns it. On 8/25 the close also sets the deliverable clock every time: findings in a readout "in about three weeks." **[parts] [reporting] [peterbilt]**
